documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
66M here to establish care, transferring from his prior primary care office. Wife with him and fills in dates.

PD: diagnosed early 2016 at age 62 after his wife noticed a tremor in his right hand and that he'd gone quiet-faced. Seen by an outside neurology group, about twice a year. On carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 TID and pramipexole ER 1.5 mg daily. Says the tremor is mostly a nuisance; buttons are slow. No falls, no freezing, no lightheadedness on standing that he notices.

CAD: had a nuclear stress test in 2016 at his old practice, ordered for vague exertional fatigue; told it was abnormal, cardiology recommended medical therapy, never had a cath. No chest pain since. Aspirin 81 and atorvastatin 20.

Lipids: on atorvastatin for years.

Hands: numb fingers both sides for a couple of years, both wrists released in early 2018; numbness gone.

Meds reconciled from bottles: carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 TID, pramipexole ER 1.5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily. NKDA.
FHx: father MI at 63. Mother had Alzheimer's. One older brother, hypertension.
SHx: retired after decades teaching high school math. Married. Never smoked, doesn't drink.

Exam: well appearing. BP and HR as recorded. Mild resting tremor R hand, reduced facial expression, slightly soft voice. Gait a bit slow, steady, turns in three steps. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. No edema. Healed volar wrist scars bilaterally.

A/P
1. Parkinson disease: stable on current regimen; continue with outside neurology. Will request their last note.
2. CAD, medically managed: asymptomatic. Continue aspirin, statin.
3. Hyperlipidemia: lipid panel today.
4. Health maintenance: prior records requested for colonoscopy and vaccine dates. High-dose flu today. HCV and HIV screening today, he agreed.
CBC, CMP, lipids, TSH drawn. Return 3 months.

- 01/2018 and 03/2018 hand surgery op notes: right then left carpal tunnel release, uncomplicated.

documents.title: Office Visit: Dysphagia
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Since around February, food and also drinks seem to hang up low behind the breastbone a few seconds after he swallows. Gets worse slowly. Sometimes has to bring a bite back up, and it comes up looking like he just ate it. Takes his pills with a lot of water now. No heartburn, no pain with swallowing, no chest pain. Weight steady by our scale and his.
Wife wondered if it's the Parkinson's; no coughing or choking with drinks, and the hold-up is low in the chest, not in the throat.
Exam: weight as recorded, unchanged. Oropharynx normal. Neck supple, no mass. Abdomen soft, nontender. Tremor unchanged.
A/P: Esophageal dysphagia to both solids and liquids, progressive. Needs GI evaluation and probably a barium study and scope. Referred to gastroenterology, asked for the next available. Small soft bites, upright after meals in the meantime. Call if he can't get liquids down.

documents.title: RE: GI appointment

documents.title: Gastroenterology Consultation (05/25/2021)
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
GASTROENTEROLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of service: 05/25/2021
Referred by: primary care

Reason: dysphagia

HPI: 67-year-old man with Parkinson disease and coronary artery disease, three months of gradually worsening dysphagia. Both solids and liquids feel delayed at the level of the lower sternum shortly after eating. Intermittent regurgitation of undigested food. Denies weight loss, chest pain and heartburn. No prior upper endoscopy, dilation or foregut surgery.

Medications: carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 mg TID; pramipexole 1.5 mg daily; atorvastatin 20 mg daily; aspirin 81 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: father with MI at 63; mother with Alzheimer disease; brother with hypertension.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol.

Exam: unremarkable. Abdomen soft, nontender, no masses.

Barium esophagram (performed today): the esophagus is dilated, with smooth symmetric tapering to a narrow "bird's beak" at the gastroesophageal junction and slow passage of contrast into the stomach. No mucosal irregularity or mass.

Impression: findings are typical of achalasia.

Plan: upper endoscopy to exclude a lesion at the gastroesophageal junction, then high-resolution esophageal manometry. We will discuss treatment options (pneumatic dilation, myotomy) once those are back.

Gastroenterology

documents.title: Cardiology Consultation (11/24/2021)
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Cardiology consultation, 11/24/2021

Thank you for referring Mr. Hickey, 68, with Parkinson disease, coronary artery disease on medical therapy, and achalasia treated with dilation this summer. He describes six months of steadily worsening breathlessness on exertion and swelling in both legs. Prior bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, released.

Medications: carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 TID, pramipexole 1.5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg, aspirin 81 mg. NKDA. Never smoker, no alcohol. Father MI at 63.

Exam: BP 130/85, HR 92. JVP elevated. S3 present, no murmurs. Lungs clear. Bilateral lower extremity edema.

Data: creatinine 1.2, BNP 900 pg/mL, urinalysis 3+ protein without blood or casts, albumin 3.2, total cholesterol 210. Echo and ECG as reported separately: thick walls with a normal-sized cavity, preserved EF, speckled myocardium; low QRS voltage with nonspecific ST-T changes.

Assessment: the mismatch between thick walls on echo and low voltage on ECG, with his carpal tunnel history, strongly suggests cardiac amyloidosis.

Plan:
1. Furosemide 20 mg each morning for the edema.
2. Technetium pyrophosphate scan; serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light chains to exclude light-chain disease.
3. If transthyretin type, TTR gene testing.
4. Return after testing.

Cardiology

Movement disorders follow-up, 11/29/2022

Mr. Hickey, 69, with Parkinson disease since 2016, plus achalasia and ATTR cardiac amyloidosis, returns with his wife. She says he hesitates when starting to move and looks stiff, most in the early morning and again late in the day. He did well on his regimen for years, but the benefit has leveled off and the slowness now limits him. He takes his carbidopa/levodopa faithfully.

ROS: appetite good. Sleeps through most nights. No weakness, no memory complaints. Independent in basic self-care.

Current: carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 TID, pramipexole 1.5 mg daily, plus his cardiac medications.

Exam: vitals normal. Finger tapping slowed bilaterally, R more than L. Hypophonic. Reduced right arm swing on gait. Affect subdued, cooperative throughout.

Labs: TSH and basic metabolic panel normal.

Impression:
1. Parkinson disease, benefit of current regimen has plateaued.
2. Mood disorder related to his Parkinson disease; subdued affect noted today, no safety concerns.

Plan: add entacapone 200 mg with each levodopa dose to strengthen the levodopa response. Ask primary care to screen mood at visits. Return in 6 months.

Neurology

documents.title: Discharge Summary: Cardiac Surgery (05/29/2024 to 06/03/2024)
documents.author: cardiac surgery
documents.body:
CARDIAC SURGERY DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 05/29/2024. Discharged: 06/03/2024.
Principal procedure: coronary artery bypass grafting with left internal mammary artery harvest, via median sternotomy, on cardiopulmonary bypass (05/29/2024).
Indication: severe multivessel coronary artery disease with exertional angina.
History: 70-year-old man with Parkinson disease, wild-type transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis on tafamidis, and achalasia treated with dilation.
Allergies: NKDA.

Hospital course: The operation itself went without incident, and he was taken to the cardiac ICU intubated. Roughly two hours after arrival the team was called for steady chest-tube output and oozing around the internal jugular line, ongoing despite several liters of crystalloid and transfusion of blood products. He had received unfractionated heparin during the case for bypass. Coagulation studies showed a prolonged aPTT with a normal PT, normal platelet count and normal fibrinogen; nothing to suggest thrombocytopenia or DIC. Bleeding was attributed to persistent heparin effect. Urgent reversal with protamine was given, and chest-tube output fell off over the following hour without return to the operating room. Extubated postoperative day 1. Chest tubes out day 3. Carbidopa/levodopa kept on schedule. Ambulating with PT by day 2. Discharged home with his wife.

Discharge diagnoses: severe multivessel CAD s/p CABG; postoperative hemorrhage due to anticoagulant (heparin), reversed; Parkinson disease; ATTR-wt cardiac amyloidosis; achalasia; hyperlipidemia.

Discharge medications: aspirin 81 mg daily; atorvastatin 20 mg daily; carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 TID; pramipexole 1.5 mg daily; tafamidis 61 mg daily; furosemide 20 mg daily. Nitroglycerin as needed.
Instructions: sternal precautions, no lifting over 10 lb, no driving 4-6 weeks. Cardiac surgery clinic in 2 weeks; primary care in 1-2 weeks; cardiac rehab referral after clearance.

Cardiac surgery

Yesterday he went to the ED because his chest was 'clicking and popping' when he moved and sore for a couple of days; they x-rayed and told him a sternal wire had moved, no infection, sent him home with instructions to protect the chest. No fever. Taking all meds; reviewed list against discharge summary, matches. Using a pillow to brace when he coughs. Visit booked 6/25 (first with PCP; surgeon visit is 6/12). Requested ED record.

documents.body: Wife called: he ran a fever over the weekend and the incision got red and started draining, so she took him to the ED Saturday. documents.title: Emergency Department Record (06/04/2024)
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Date: 06/04/2024
CC: chest wall popping with movement, mild chest pain x 2 days

HPI: 70M, CABG on 5/29, discharged yesterday. For two days has felt the front of his chest pop or click when he moves or turns in bed, with mild soreness. Denies fever, cough, shortness of breath.
PMH: Parkinson disease, ATTR cardiac amyloidosis, achalasia, CAD s/p CABG, hyperlipidemia.
Meds: per discharge list. NKDA.

Exam: T 37.2 C (99 F), BP 130/85, P 88, RR 16. Comfortable. Sternotomy incision closed and intact, no erythema, no drainage. Palpable clicking over the sternum with discomfort on palpation. Lungs clear.

Labs: WBC 7,500, Hgb 13.2, platelets 250,000, CRP 8 mg/L.
CXR: displaced sternal wire.

MDM: sternal instability with wire displacement, early postoperative; no clinical sign of infection. Discussed by phone with cardiac surgery on call: sternal precautions, chest support, keep surgical clinic follow-up, return for fever, redness or drainage.
Dx: superficial surgical wound dehiscence (sternal).
Disposition: home with wife.

Emergency medicine

results.text: Staphylococcus aureus, methicillin-susceptible (oxacillin susceptible; cefazolin susceptible)

reports.text: Median sternotomy wires again noted. Small fluid collection anterior to the sternum. Lungs clear without consolidation. No pneumothorax.

Postoperative sternotomy. Fluid collection anterior to the sternum, corresponding to the radiograph finding. Lungs without consolidation. No pleural effusion of significance. Mediastinal structures otherwise as expected after recent cardiac surgery.
reports.conclusion: Fluid collection anterior to the sternum after recent sternotomy.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record (06/08/2024)
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Date: 06/08/2024
CC: fever, malaise, red painful sternal wound

HPI: 70M, postoperative day 10 from CABG, seen here on 6/4 for sternal wire displacement. Low-grade fevers began three days ago and have climbed. Feels unwell. Increasing redness and pain at the incision.
Meds per list. NKDA.

Exam: T 38.9 C (102 F), HR 110, BP 130/85. Ill-appearing. Sternal incision erythematous with purulent drainage; swelling and tenderness over the sternum.

Labs: WBC 15,000, Hgb 12.5, CRP 24 mg/L. Blood cultures x2 drawn.
CXR: small fluid collection in front of the sternum. CT chest: corresponding anterior collection.

Assessment: postoperative mediastinitis. Cardiac surgery at bedside; admitted to their service. Empiric IV antibiotics started after cultures.

Emergency medicine

documents.title: Discharge Summary: Cardiac Surgery (06/08/2024 to 06/20/2024)
documents.author: cardiac surgery
documents.body:
CARDIAC SURGERY DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 06/08/2024. Discharged: 06/20/2024.
Diagnosis: postoperative mediastinitis after CABG (5/29/2024), with preceding sternal wound dehiscence.
Procedure: 06/09/2024 sternal debridement, mediastinal washout and sternal rewiring.

Course: Taken to the OR the morning after admission. Infected tissue at the sternal wound was debrided and the mediastinum irrigated; sternum rewired and closed. Operative culture grew methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Blood cultures no growth. Empiric IV antibiotics narrowed to cefazolin on culture data. Fever resolved by day 3. PICC placed 6/14. Wound clean at discharge. Parkinson medications given on time throughout.

Discharge medications: cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours via PICC through 7/21/2024 (6 weeks from debridement), home infusion arranged; aspirin 81 mg; atorvastatin 20 mg; carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 TID; pramipexole 1.5 mg daily; tafamidis 61 mg; furosemide 20 mg.
Follow-up: weekly CBC and BMP drawn by home infusion nursing, results to cardiac surgery and primary care. Cardiac surgery clinic 7/22. PCP within a week.

Cardiac surgery

documents.title: Transitional Care Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen with wife after two hospital stays: CABG 5/29 (bleeding from residual heparin in the ICU, reversed with protamine), ED 6/4 for a displaced sternal wire, then readmitted 6/8 to 6/20 for mediastinitis, debrided and rewired 6/9, MSSA, on IV cefazolin through 7/21.
Now: tired but better each day. No fevers at home. Home infusion nurse comes weekly. Eating fine, swallowing OK. No chest pressure at all since surgery; hasn't needed nitroglycerin. Walking the hallway and driveway.
Meds reconciled with both discharge lists: cefazolin IV q8h, aspirin, atorvastatin 20, carbidopa/levodopa TID, pramipexole ER 1.5, tafamidis, furosemide. Stopping SL nitroglycerin per surgery.
Exam: afebrile. Vitals as recorded. Sternal incision clean and dry, no drainage, edges together. R arm PICC site clean, no redness. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Trace ankle edema.
A/P
1. Mediastinitis s/p debridement, on cefazolin: improving; weekly infusion labs to us.
2. CABG: postoperative bleeding episode resolved.
3. Anemia from surgery: recovering per infusion labs.
4. PD, ATTR-wt amyloid: continue regimen.
Cardiac surgery 7/22. Return here in 3 months, sooner if needed.

Cardiac surgery postoperative clinic, 07/22/2024

Completed six weeks of IV cefazolin yesterday. PICC removed today, tip intact. Afebrile, energy improving.
Exam: sternotomy healed; no erythema or drainage. Sternum stable on cough and palpation, no click.
Impression: mediastinitis treated; sternal dehiscence repaired and healed.
Plan: lifting restrictions relaxed gradually over the next month. Cardiac rehab referral placed. Back to cardiology and primary care for ongoing care; surgical follow-up as needed.

Cardiac surgery

orders.reason: Orthopnea and paradoxical abdominal motion after CABG

documents.title: Office Visit: Orthopnea
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Since the surgery he hasn't been able to lie flat without feeling short of breath; sleeps propped on pillows. Tires with exertion more than he'd expect after finishing rehab. His own observation: when he takes a big breath, his belly pulls in instead of out. No ankle swelling beyond his usual trace, weight steady, no chest pressure, no fever, no cough.
Exam: vitals as recorded. Lying back to 30 degrees, visible inward movement of the upper abdomen on inspiration. Breath sounds reduced at the L base. Heart regular. Sternotomy healed. Trace edema.
PHQ-9 7: tired, less interest; no safety concerns. Still prefers no counseling.
A/P: Orthopnea with paradoxical abdominal motion after cardiac surgery: concern for diaphragm weakness rather than worsening amyloid heart disease (weight and edema unchanged). Referred to pulmonology. Wife to send weights if they climb.

conditions.note: Left; paralysis of left hemidiaphragm after CABG

reports.text: Median sternotomy wires intact. The left hemidiaphragm is elevated. Lungs otherwise clear. No pleural effusion. Heart size within normal limits.

documents.title: Pulmonology Consultation (12/02/2024) and Sniff Test (12/10/2024)
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
PULMONARY CONSULTATION, 12/02/2024

Mr. Hickey is 71, with Parkinson disease, wild-type ATTR cardiac amyloidosis, and CABG in May complicated by mediastinitis. Since his surgery he has trouble breathing when lying flat and fatigue with exertion, worse over the last two months. He notices his abdomen moving in when he breathes deeply.
Never smoker. NKDA. Medications per your list.

Exam: abdomen moves inward on inspiration, supine. Breath sounds decreased at the left base. Heart regular. Sternum healed.

Data: Hgb 13.8, WBC 7,200, platelets 250,000; electrolytes normal. Room-air arterial gas: pH 7.42, PaCO2 44, PaO2 72, HCO3 24. Chest x-ray: elevated left hemidiaphragm.

Assessment: left phrenic nerve injury after cardiac surgery, with left hemidiaphragm dysfunction explaining the orthopnea.

Plan: fluoroscopic sniff test. Sleep with the head of the bed raised. Phrenic injuries after cardiac surgery often recover over months; recheck in six months before discussing anything further.

Addendum, 12/10/2024, fluoroscopic sniff test: paradoxical upward motion of the left hemidiaphragm with sniffing; right hemidiaphragm moves normally. Consistent with left hemidiaphragm paralysis. Plan unchanged.

Pulmonology

documents.title: Cardiology Annual Follow-up (02/11/2025)
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Amyloid clinic, 02/11/2025

Seen nine months after CABG, complicated course noted (postoperative bleeding, sternal infection, left phrenic nerve injury followed by pulmonology). No angina since surgery. Exertional breathlessness at his pre-surgery baseline; still sleeps propped up, which pulmonology attributes to the diaphragm. Ankles controlled.
Exam: vitals normal. Regular, no murmur. JVP normal. Healed sternotomy. No edema.
Impression: ATTR-wt cardiomyopathy, stable on tafamidis; CAD s/p CABG without angina.
Plan: continue tafamidis 61 mg, furosemide 20 mg, aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg. One year.

Cardiology

AWV, afternoon slot as he prefers. Wife present.
Interval: CABG last May with a rough recovery, now done with rehab. Left diaphragm paralysis per pulmonology; still sleeps on a wedge. Cardiology letter from February reviewed.
Function: independent in self-care; wife handles driving now beyond town. No falls. TUG 14 s. Mini-Cog 5/5.
PHQ-9 6. Declines counseling again; says getting through the surgery 'took something out of him.'
Meds: carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 TID, pramipexole ER 1.5 mg, tafamidis 61 mg, furosemide 20 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg, aspirin 81 mg. NKDA.
Exam: hypomimia, R rest tremor, mild rigidity R wrist. Sternotomy healed. Heart regular. Breath sounds reduced L base. Trace ankle edema.
Prevention: Tdap today (last 2014). Flu and COVID done in the fall. Colonoscopy due 2027; will revisit given age and health at that time.
Labs today. Return in 4 months.

documents.title: Question about Ron
documents.author: patient
documents.body: This is Ron's wife writing on his account. For a few weeks he has been seeing people in the yard who are not there, and he is convinced the neighbors are coming in and taking things from the garage. He is otherwise himself, no fever, eating fine. He has his neurology appointment June 8. Should we wait for that?

documents.title: RE: Question about Ron
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thank you for telling us. Keeping the June 8 neurology visit makes sense; I'll let their office know what you've described so they're prepared. If he becomes confused, feverish, unusually sleepy, or you feel unsafe, call us the same day or go to the ED. Please don't change any of his medications on your own before then.

conditions.label: Parkinson disease with psychosis
conditions.note: Visual hallucinations and paranoid ideation; per neurology

documents.title: Neurology Visit (06/08/2026)
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
Movement disorders clinic, 06/08/2026

Mr. Hickey, 72, with Parkinson disease, wild-type ATTR cardiac amyloidosis, CABG in 2024 with a complicated course, and achalasia. His wife brings him in for a month of visual hallucinations and rising suspicion of the neighbors, whom he accuses of stealing from him. His regimen has been stable: carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 TID and pramipexole 1.5 mg daily. Motor symptoms are well controlled; no change in movement.

Exam: vitals normal. Alert, oriented to person, place and time. Rest tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity as before. No signs of infection or delirium.

Impression: Parkinson disease psychosis.

Plan:
1. Taper pramipexole, the most likely contributor: 0.75 mg ER daily for two weeks, then stop. Continue carbidopa/levodopa unchanged.
2. Primary care to check CBC, metabolic panel, TSH, B12 and urinalysis to exclude a medical contributor.
3. Recheck here in three months, sooner if symptoms escalate.

Neurology

documents.title: Office Visit: Hallucinations
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
With wife. Neurology note from 6/8 received and reviewed: Parkinson disease psychosis; plan to taper pramipexole and for us to check labs.
Since then: still sees figures at the edge of the yard most evenings; mostly not bothered by them. Accused the neighbor once more about a missing rake (wife found it in the shed). Sleep OK. No fever, cough, urinary symptoms, constipation beyond his usual. No new medicines or supplements; no sleep aids or anything over the counter.
Exam: afebrile, vitals as recorded. Alert, attentive, oriented x3; conversation linear; he describes the figures calmly. Rest tremor R, bradykinesia, rigidity as before. Heart regular. Lungs: reduced L base, unchanged. Abdomen soft. No edema beyond trace.
A/P
1. PD psychosis: following neurology's plan. Pramipexole ER reduced to 0.75 mg daily x 2 weeks then off; new script sent and old dose stopped. Carbidopa/levodopa unchanged. Wife to call if worse, if he wanders or she feels unsafe.
2. Medical contributors: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, UA today.
Phone check at the end of the taper.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Ron and family: all of Tuesday's tests are normal, including blood counts, sodium, calcium, kidney and liver tests, thyroid, B12, and the urine test. Nothing medical is driving the hallucinations, which supports neurology's plan. Continue the lower pramipexole dose until the 30th.

documents.title: Taper check
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Spoke with Ron and wife. Last 0.75 mg dose today; stops tomorrow as neurology planned. Motor symptoms no different, no falls. Hallucinations perhaps less nightly. Pramipexole removed from med list. Visit in mid-August, sooner if motor symptoms worsen much or hallucinations escalate. Neurology updated by fax.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
With wife, seven weeks off pramipexole. Hallucinations now a few times a week, usually at dusk; he recognizes they aren't real and lets them go. No accusations against the neighbors for about three weeks. Motor function the same as before the taper by both their accounts.
PHQ-9 6.
Exam: alert, oriented, linear. Rest tremor R, bradykinesia, mild rigidity, unchanged. Heart regular. Lungs: reduced L base. Trace edema.
A/P
1. PD psychosis: improving after stopping pramipexole. Carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 TID unchanged. Neurology recheck booked for September.
2. ATTR-wt amyloid, CAD s/p CABG, L phrenic injury, achalasia: stable.
3. Mood: unchanged mild symptoms.
Return in September after neurology.
